title: Computing key rates for one-sided device-independent quantum key distribution
authors: Andreas Bluhm, Gereon Koßmann, Martin Sandfuchs, René Schwonnek, Giuseppe Viola, Ramona Wolf
abstract: The defining feature of one-sided device-independent quantum key distribution is its asymmetric trust model in which only one party is characterized. This scenario sets an interesting middle ground between high key rates achievable by characterizing devices and the security of full device-independence. Here, we provide new tools, methods, and benchmarks for calculating key rates in this setting. To achieve this, we develop and compare two extensions of the NPA hierarchy and derive finite-size security bounds against general attacks with arbitrary device memory. The latter is based on the Generalized Entropy Accumulation Theorem. We then investigate the performance of various protocols: the BB84 protocol both with and without losses, a qutrit mutually unbiased bases protocol, and protocols based on Bell inequalties such as CHSH and $I_{3322}$. We find that the choice of which party is characterized can strongly affects the key rate, surprisingly without a universal ordering. Our work thus offers a general toolbox for calculating key rates for one-sided device-independent QKD protocols.
summary: This work provides a comprehensive mathematical toolbox for calculating key rates in one-sided device-independent Quantum Key Distribution (DIQKD). By extending the NPA hierarchy and using advanced algebraic techniques, the authors solve the key rate problem as a complex optimization over C*-algebras. The results highlight that the security performance is critically dependent on the asymmetric placement of trust between the two communicating parties.
main_problem: The paper focuses on developing general tools and methods to calculate the achievable secret key rates for one-sided device-independent quantum key distribution (DIQKD).
main_result: The key rate calculation is shown to be highly dependent on which party's device is characterized, demonstrating no universal ordering for optimal trust placement.
method: The authors develop extensions of the NPA hierarchy and utilize the Generalized Entropy Accumulation Theorem (GEAT) to formulate the key rate problem as a non-commutative polynomial optimization over C*-algebras.
model_or_system: The model is the one-sided DIQKD setting, characterized by an asymmetric trust model where one party's device is fully characterized while the other is treated as a black box.
key_observables: Achievable secret key rate ($r_\infty$), conditional von Neumann entropy ($H(S|IQE)_ho - H(S|IB)_ho$).
important_parameters: The choice of which party (Alice or Bob) is characterized; the size of the key ($n$) for finite-size bounds.
main_assumptions: The public information ($I$) must not depend on the memory of the untrusted device; the analysis relies on advanced algebraic structures like C*-algebras and the NPA hierarchy extensions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates different levels of device characterization in QKD (Device-dependent, DIQKD, One-sided DIQKD). Figure 2 shows the setup for one-sided DIQKD, distinguishing between the characterized and black-boxed measurement devices.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the one-sided DIQKD setting and the key rate optimization problem (using entropy bounds) to developing advanced mathematical tools. These tools involve extending the NPA hierarchy and establishing rigorous algebraic isomorphisms between the measurement constraints and tensor products of algebras.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework developed—linking key rate computation to C*-algebraic optimization—provides powerful, general tools applicable to analyzing security in various quantum communication protocols beyond simple qubit systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Different levels of device characterisation in QKD protocols. Device-dependent QKD (a) assumes fully characterised measurement devices for both parties A and B, whereas DIQKD (b) requires no assumptions about the devices and relies only on observed correlations. One-sided DIQKD (c) represents an intermediate scenario, where one measurement device is characterised while the other is treated as a black box.

Figure 2: Setup for one-sided DIQKD. An untrusted source distributes a quantum state to Alice and Bob, who perform local measurements and exchange classical information I. One measurement device is treated as a black box, indicated by the question mark, while the other is fully characterised, denoted by M or N for Alice or Bob, respectively. Throughout this work, Alice generates the raw key S. The choice of which party’s measurement device is characterised is part of the protocol specification.

Figure 3: Plot of the asymptotic key rate as a function of the depolarizing probability q. Shown are the cases when Bob is trusted (and Alice is not), the case when Alice is trusted (and Bob is not), and when neither party is trusted (fully device-independent). In all cases, the key is extracted from Alice’s measurement results.

Figure 4: Key rates for the one-sided device-independent BB84 protocol with trusted Alice as a function of Alice’s detection efficiency ηA for different values of the depolarizing probability q and the number of rounds n. Bob’s detection efficiency is fixed at ηB = 0.8 and he assigns non-detection events to the outcome b = 0. The testing probability is fixed at γ = 0.1. The soundness parameter is set to εsnd = 10−12 and the completeness parameter is set to εcomp = 0.01.

Figure 5: Key rates for the one-sided DIQKD protocol based on d + 1 mutually unbiased bases in d-dimensional Hilbert spaces. We compare bounds derived via the von Neumann entropy with bounds based on the min-entropy. The former are calculated using our method based on the KS objective function and the NPA-MP hierarchy, whereas for the latter we used the SDP relaxation of the min- entropy from [MGG+26]. We observe that even in dimension d = 3, the von Neumann entropy provides better noise tolerance than the min-entropy at d = 7.
